Neonates of the Lancet fish (Notoscopelus kroyeri) emerge from their pelagic eggs at an extraordinarily small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.000014 grams [Wwb = 0.000014 grams]. This minute initial mass, typical of myctophid larvae, is derived from an egg diameter of approximately 0.3 millimeters and reflects a yolk-dependent strategy common among mesopelagic teleosts. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that must occur before the point of no return is reached. Growth during the early larval stages is rapid, driven by the productive waters of the North Atlantic where this species is predominantly found. The larva progresses through flexion and postflexion stages, undergoing a dramatic increase in body mass as it transitions from a planktonic to a more active, free-swimming lifestyle. The physical environment, particularly temperature, plays a decisive role in mediating these early developmental rates, with metabolic processes being tightly coupled to the ambient thermal regime experienced in the upper mesopelagic zone.

Field surveys and laboratory-based growth reconstructions have provided robust estimates for the somatic development of Notoscopelus kroyeri throughout its juvenile phase. Individuals typically attain sexual maturation upon reaching a standard length of 9.2 centimeters [Lp = 9.2 centimeters], a measurement that defines the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the transition to adulthood. At this pubertal stage, the wet weight is approximately 4.53 grams [Wwp = approximately 4.53 grams], reflecting an allometric relationship between length and mass that is consistent with that observed in other lanternfishes. The journey from a 0.000014 gram hatchling to a 4.53 gram maturing individual involves an enormous multiplicative increase in biomass, representing several orders of magnitude of growth over a period of several months. During this sub-adult phase, the fish must successfully navigate predation pressure and food limitation in the deep scattering layer, accumulating sufficient lipid reserves to support the energetic demands of future reproduction. The progressive development of the gonads becomes histologically evident as the fish approaches the 9.2 centimeter threshold, with vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis initiating shortly thereafter.

Under the persistent thermal conditions of 6.8 °C [T = 6.8 °C] that define their bathypelagic habitat, mature females exhibit a remarkable annual reproductive output, with field estimates suggesting that each female produces approximately 85,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 85,000 eggs per year]. This high fecundity positions Notoscopelus kroyeri among the more productive members of its genus. The continuous production of small, pelagic eggs is an adaptive strategy that maximizes the probability of offspring encountering favorable conditions in a variable mesopelagic environment. The sustained high reproductive output is likely supported by the efficient nutrient absorption from a diet dominated by copepods and euphausiids. The 6.8 °C thermal regime at depth presumably optimizes the metabolic efficiency of oogenesis, allowing for the maintenance of this prodigious fecundity over the course of multiple spawning cycles throughout the year.

Adult body size in Notoscopelus kroyeri is characterized by an ultimate standard length of 14.3 centimeters [Li = 14.3 centimeters], which represents the maximum recorded length for this species in the wild. This terminal length is associated with an ultimate wet weight of 19.56 grams [Wwi = 19.56 grams], as derived from length-mass regressions applied to large, presumably senescent individuals. This asymptotic size is modest compared to some larger myctophid species but is typical for members of the genus Notoscopelus that inhabit temperate and subpolar waters. The growth trajectory to this maximum size is gradual, with the fish continuing to add somatic tissue even after reaching maturity, albeit at a decelerating rate. The ultimate body mass of 19.56 grams [Wwi = 19.56 grams] represents a trade-off between the energetic costs of further growth and the benefits of increased fecundity, which scales positively with body size in most teleosts. Large, old individuals are comparatively rare in sampled populations, likely due to a combination of natural mortality and the energetic demands of sustained reproductive effort at depth.

Under the persistent thermal conditions of 6.8 °C [T = 6.8 °C] that define their bathypelagic habitat, Lancet fish exhibit a maximum documented lifespan of approximately 2,190 days [am = approximately 2,190 days]. This longevity of roughly six years is considerable for a small mesopelagic fish and suggests a life-history strategy characterized by relatively slow senescence and iteroparous reproduction over multiple seasons. The extended lifespan allows females to accumulate multiple years of reproductive output, partially compensating for the high mortality rates experienced during the early pelagic larval phase. The cold environment slows metabolic aging processes, contributing to this protracted life span compared to epipelagic species of similar body size. Tagging studies and otolith microchemistry have corroborated these longevity estimates, with the oldest verified individuals consistently falling near the six-year mark. This combination of a modest 19.56 gram ultimate wet weight and a multi-year reproductive window underscores a conservative, energy-efficient adaptation to the stable but resource-limited deep-ocean environment.
